notes.text: I'm starting by pulling up the mission briefing to see what the task involves.

I'm laying out the plan: six unknowns, with the wind at aircraft altitude giving speed and direction there, test drops at 100 m giving the surface wind directly, and drops at two other heights to estimate shear and veer. Since each wind reading is noisy, I'm thinking several measurements will help, and I'm now turning to how drag will be pinned down from fall time and horizontal drift.

Now I'm working through the drag estimate and the test-drop layout: releasing loads well away from the fire, roughly 300 m to the east, at three altitudes so the wind profile can be pinned down.

I'm working through the wind profile numbers: 6.2 m/s at 100 m from 32°, 6.5 at 150 m from 28°, and 4.1 at 30 m from 50°. The log-law shear exponents come out around 0.12 between 100 and 150 m and 0.34 between 30 and 100 m, with a noisy 0.5 m/s spread, so an average near 0.3 is my rough estimate. The direction veers by about 18° from 30 m up to 100 m.

I'm working out the veer between heights: about -26° per 100 m from 30 to 100 m, and -8° per 100 m from 100 to 150 m, with roughly 4° of noise, so I'm leaning toward a veer near -20°. The fall time from 100 m is slow enough that I suspect large drag, so I'll try fitting it directly against the observations.
The fall time looks too long, which points to drag being set too high. The along-track distance falls short of the observed eastward offset, so I'll lower the drag and try 0.025.

I'm estimating the drag-coefficient zero by linearly interpolating the time-step values for both drops, which lands around 0.027. The same interpolation on drop 1's horizontal offset is still underway.

I'm checking the drop 2 and drop 3 vertical offsets against the same interpolation, and drop 3 comes out at 0.025, though it's a short 30 m drop. Trying 0.027 next, since the cross-track errors are still small.

Most of the y-residuals sit near +2, so the predicted positions are running too far north. That points to the wind's north component being slightly too strong, or just measurement noise of about 1.5 m. The x-residual near -1.5 on the short eastward leg is smaller and I'll set it aside for now. The wind speed, shear and veer still aren't pinned down, so I need more drops to constrain them.

The wind and shear are still the weak point: drift over a 3 to 10 second fall at about 6 m/s adds up to metres, so I need the remaining test drops to pin those down. Drops from the highest release altitude give the longest fall and the most wind sensitivity. The updraft through the smoke column near the fire centre also lengthens the fall and shifts the impact, so I have to account for it in the operational drops too.

I'm checking the updraft at the fire centre: at its peak it could reach about 21 m/s, which exceeds the roughly 19 m/s terminal velocity, so it might hold the load up. Next I'll calibrate it with a test drop aimed at the origin, released from the spot that would land there without updraft, and see how much the column shifts the impact.

I'm weighing how many updraft calibration drops to run, and I think one smoke drop is enough since the updraft is a single parameter. I'll also fit wind measurements at other altitudes, since each test drop yields a wind reading at its release height. So the next step is a smoke drop from 100 m, plus a separate drop from 60 m away from the column.

Drop 4 took 8.34 seconds against 7.11 for the earlier one, so there's a real updraft. Wind at 100 m averages 5.9 m/s at about 34.5°, while at 60 m it's 4.6 at 46°, at 30 m 4.1 at 50°, and at 150 m 6.5 at 28°. Working the shear from the 100 m and 60 m readings, I get about 0.49, and from 100 m down to 30 m about 1.

Now I'm working out the vertical wind shear from the 30 m, 60 m, and 150 m readings, which comes to about 0.3 on average. The veer between levels runs roughly -13 to -29 degrees, around -20 overall. Then I'll set these against the drag of 0.027, the 5.9 m/s wind from 34 degrees, and the updraft of about 5.
Drop 4 came in at -0.27, so there isn't enough updraft. I'll try updraft 7 next.

I'm checking where the zero crossing falls, roughly at dt ≈ 5.9, and reading off the y-offset there, about 3.2. That puts the prediction about 3 too far north, so I'm suspecting the north wind component is too strong, possibly the wind direction itself, since the time spent in the column is longer. I'll try an updraft of 5.9 and then tune the wind.

I'm going through the drops one by one, and the x-offsets look consistently short, so the wind's east component seems too weak at low altitude. The y-scatter is noisy enough that I won't lean on it. I'll try rotating the wind direction toward the east at low levels to 36 degrees, keeping the updraft at 5.9.

I'm working out the direction change from 34 to 40 for each drop, comparing their x and y offsets. Drop 4 sits off the interpolated position, so its correction is larger than the others.

I'm weighing whether a stronger negative veer, with less wind at high altitude and more at low, would close the gap, and I'm considering a direction of about 36 with veer at -30. Rather than guess, I want a linear model over direction, veer, shear, wind speed, and drag, fit by finite-difference runs. I'll start from a baseline and perturb veer, shear, wind speed, and drag one at a time.

I'm setting up a linear model, starting with a baseline residual vector of per-drop shifts (dx, dy, dt) for drops 1 through 5, and I'm beginning to list the sensitivities for the direction change of +6°.

Now I'm working through the sensitivities for the remaining parameters, comparing how each one moves the per-drop residuals for veer, shear, wind speed, and drag.

I'm setting the drag value aside for now and turning to the wind fit. The along-track drag effect is still a factor, but I'm holding drag fixed. I'm treating the direction, veer, shear, and wind speed changes as unknowns, and I'm writing the first residual equations for drop 1 in the x and y directions.

I'm writing out the residual equations for drops 2 through 5 in both the x and y directions, each one combining the baseline offset with the direction, veer, shear, and wind speed terms.

I'm checking the noise level: the baseline mean miss of 1.98 is consistent with 1.5 m per-axis noise, so the fit is already near the noise floor. I'm now running a rough least-squares guess, starting with veer more negative since that improved the mean miss.

I'm setting up the normal equations for the four unknowns, listing the direction, veer, shear, and wind speed columns across the ten residual equations.

I'm computing the dot products of the direction column with the other columns to fill in the normal equations.

I'm computing the remaining dot products for the normal equations, the veer and shear columns against each other and against the wind speed column, along with the shear column's self-product.

Now I'm computing the remaining dot products for the normal equations: the wind speed column against the residuals and the remaining pairs, which are mostly large values.

I'm reducing the system by substituting the first equation into the second, which gives me an expression for a in terms of b, c, and d.

I'm reducing the system further, substituting the expression for a into the second and third equations to eliminate it and get relations between b, c, and d.

I'm reducing the normal equations further, eliminating the remaining unknowns one by one to leave a relation between c and d.

I'm solving the reduced system by back-substitution: the last pair of equations gives d ≈ 0.13 and c ≈ -0.08, and from those I'm working out b and then a.

I've worked out the solution: drop direction comes to about 34.6°, veer to roughly -29°, shear to about 0.31, and wind speed to about 6.0. I'm checking that against the wind measurements, and the speed and veer both fall within their ranges, so I'm going to compare this against the alternative hypothesis.

The mean miss came out at 1.16, which is below the noise level, though that may be a bit of overfitting. The drop 4 dy of 2.2 still bugs me: it shifted about +1.9 when updraft changed by +2, and dt moved 0.6 for the same change. Updraft itself comes from dt with roughly ±0.17 uncertainty, so that 2.2 might just be noise at about 1.5σ. Next I'm turning to the remaining five test drops.

I'm planning the next test drops: one from 150 m heading 0 at speed 80, released from the mirrored point, and one from 30 m heading 180 at speed 45, to probe updraft and wind at the extremes of the altitude range.

Both drops at 100 and 150 came out with the predicted position too far north. Since they were in smoke, I'm wondering whether the north wind component kept them in the smoke longer and so drifted them further, and whether a slightly lower updraft would shorten that time.

I'm wondering whether testing a slightly different updraft, around 5.5, and nudging the wind direction would show how sensitive the drift is, since the time spent in smoke might be what's pushing the predictions north.

I'm checking the dt values, and 5.9 comes out better than 5.5, with residuals near zero there, so I'll keep 5.9. The optimum looks to be around 5.85. Next I'm looking at the dy residual in the smoke drops and wondering whether low-altitude wind or the time spent near the ground in the smoke column explains it, especially since the updraft weakens below about 15 m.

I'm checking the dy residuals of about 2 m, roughly 1.3σ, which seems acceptable but might mean the north wind component is a bit off. Before using the three remaining test drops, I want to keep in mind that begin_operation can't be undone, so I'm planning to spend them on conditions that tell me the most: smoke drops at different headings and altitudes. I'm starting to sketch the first one, a heading-270 drop from 125 m at speed 50, aiming to land near the origin.

I'm working out how to simulate the remaining three drops, the ones with headings 135 and 225 at the other altitudes and speeds. Since releasing straight over the fire would pass through the column, I'll simulate from a point well away from it and use those displacements.

I'm working out the release positions for each drop: drop 8 and drop 9 flip to the opposite side of the origin, and drop 10 is released inside the column at about 21.7 m from the center. That one starts at 150 m in the updraft, so it's a strong test.
I used all three and didn't hold one back, so I'll need to go back and sort that out. Now I'm comparing the options.

I'm checking whether the drop 8 and 10 residuals point to a higher updraft, since the predicted landing for drop 8 sits about 4.2 units off from the observed impact. I'm also noting the predicted position for drop 10 and starting to tally the dt residuals for those two drops.

I'm comparing the dt residuals across drops 8, 9, 6 and 4, and noting that drops 8 and 10 have slow speeds, so they spend longer in the column. Next I want to refit with drag and updraft included, which means new sensitivities for all ten drops using six perturbations plus the baseline I already have.

I'm setting up a least squares fit with six parameters across 30 observations of dx, dy, and dt. I'm weighting dt by 30 so its 0.05 s noise is on the same footing as the 1.5 m position noise, and I'm starting from baseline residuals for the first observations.

Now I'm working through the sensitivity values for the updraft and drag terms across the observations.

Now I'm working through the weighted residuals for the remaining observations, checking the ws sensitivities for each one.

Now I'm listing the projected A and S values for the remaining observations, along with the dir sensitivity entries for points 4 through 10.

Now I'm listing the veer sensitivities for the first several observations, with the dt components scaled to match.

I'm checking how the updraft and drag sensitivities split across the drops: updraft alone can't account for the shortfall on drops 8 and 10, so I'm looking at whether more drag would lengthen their fall enough.

I'm checking whether updraft and drag together can account for the slow drops 8 and 10 falling short. Combining them, the drag reduction offsets part of the updraft effect, but drops 8 and 10 still come out with the largest positive shifts.

I'm checking whether updraft and drag alone can push drops 8 and 10 up by about six units while leaving drops 4 and 6 near zero, and the answer looks like no. I'm now going to set up the full least squares over all six parameters and solve it directly instead of guessing.

Rather than plugging in the long sensitivity listings, I'll just set up the normal equations over all six parameters and solve them directly.

Writing the weight vectors for the updraft, drag, and wind terms across the observations...

Still writing out the sensitivity vectors for the least squares setup...

Still writing out the residual and sensitivity vectors for the least squares setup...

I'm weighing whether a higher updraft could fix the slow drops 8 and 10 without throwing off the positions, since their timing residuals are about -0.2 s while their position residuals are large.

Now I'm checking whether more wind or a lower shear could pull the predicted positions of drops 8 and 10 back toward the observed ones, since their predicted landings sit too far east.

Now I'm computing the dot products for the updraft column, starting with its sum of squares and its cross-terms against the drag column.

Now I'm computing the dot products for the updraft column against the drag and wind columns, summing those cross-terms across the drops.

Now I'm computing the dot products of the updraft column against the drag, wind, and shear columns, adding up the cross-terms across the drops.

Now I'm computing the dot products of the updraft column against the drag, wind, acceleration, shear, and veer columns, summing their cross-terms across the drops.

Now I'm working out the dot products for the drag column, computing each one's sum of squares and its cross-terms with the other columns across the drops.

Still working through the G-column cross-products against W, summing each drop's contribution.

Still computing the dot products for the G column, now against the A and S columns across the drops.

Still working through the G-column dot products, now against the S column across the drops.

Now I'm computing the dot products of the drag column against the veer column, starting with the drops 1 through 9 terms.

Now I'm checking the dot products of the drag column against the gradient-related terms, tallying the residual contributions for drops 1 through 10.

Now I'm working out the weighted sums of squares for the W column, adding each drop's contribution.

Now I'm tallying the W-column products against the A column, and the first few drops' contributions are already in.

Still working through the W-column dot products, now summing the W·S terms across the drops.

Now I'm finishing the W-column dot products, tallying the per-drop W·V contributions as I go.

Still working through the W-col

I'm checking whether the mean miss of 1.79 is within the expected noise of about 1.88, keeping in mind that six parameters were fit across twenty position equations, which should push the residual somewhat lower. I'm also comparing against the earlier hypothesis, which fit the first seven well at 1.16 but did poorly on 8 and 10. Next I'm adding up the squared residuals for each position.

Now I'm totaling the squared residuals across all ten positions and the time-offset terms, which comes to about 62.5 over 30 observations, roughly 2.6 per observation against a noise variance of 2.25. That looks consistent with noise. I'm also noting that the wind measurement at 150 m sits about 2.2σ off the average of its three readings.

I'm setting up a linear fit of wind direction against height, with each measurement's direction tied to its height relative to 100 m, and I've already started averaging the directions at each level.

I'm working through the sum of the cross-terms for the wind direction regression, getting a running total of about -2,400 so far.

I'm checking the wind-direction slope from the measurements: about -0.161 degrees per metre, which gives a veer near -16 per 100 m with a standard error around ±3. The drop-fit veer is roughly -25 to -29, so the two disagree, and I'm wondering whether the drop data carries more weight.

I'm comparing the drop-fit veer of about -25 ± 3.7 against the wind-measurement veer of about -16 ± 2.8, which is roughly a 2σ gap. I'm starting to weight the two estimates together by their inverse variances to see where a combined value lands.

I'm now fitting a power law to the speed data, taking logs of the speeds and of height relative to 100 m, and I've started listing the log values at each level.

I'm working through a power-law fit to the speed data, taking logs of speeds and of relative height, and starting the sums for the regression slope.

I'm continuing the regression sums for the speed power-law fit, working through the cross-products of the log-speed deviations and the log-height deviations, and the running total is starting to build up.

I'm working out the combined wind-speed estimate from the power-law regression, which gives about 5.89 m/s with a shear around 0.32, and comparing that to the drop-fit values of 5.64 and 0.24.

I'm now wondering whether the drop-fit and wind-measurement disagreement on the shear and the veer is real or comes from nonlinearity in the fit, since the uncertainties from the normal equations are tangled up with the correlations between parameters.

I'm going to try a combined approach: a hypothesis that leans toward the wind-measurement values, with speed 5.85, shear 0.30, veer -20, direction 35, drag 0.02675, and updraft 6.2, and then check how the drop residuals compare.

Now I'm summing the squared differences at each position, pairing them up as I go.

I'm checking the total squared error for this hypothesis, which comes to about 77.9 against 62.5 for the drop fit, a difference of roughly 6.8 in chi-squared units. Comparing the wind measurements, the residuals are smaller under this hypothesis, so the two are close overall. I think a compromise between them is reasonable, and I want to check the operational predictions next.

I'm folding the wind measurements into the final least-squares fit, writing each wind residual as a linear function of the parameters around the current base. Speed sensitivity is the power-law factor (z/100) raised to the shear exponent, and the direction terms scale with height relative to 100 m.

I'm computing the speed residuals at the current base point for each measurement height, using the power-law profile with the base wind speed and shear exponent. Most residuals are small, though the 60 m and 100 m points show the largest misfits.

Now I'm checking the direction residuals at each height, and the ones at 150 m stand out as large, which points to the veer being less negative than the base value.

Now I'm setting up the speed rows of the fit, scaling each wind residual by the weight and working out how each one responds to the wind speed and shear terms at heights of 30, 60 and 100 m.

Now I'm writing out the speed and direction rows of the scaled fit, with the sensitivities to wind speed and shear at each height.

Now I'm adding the weighted wind terms into the normal matrix, summing the squared sensitivities at each height so the totals come to about 84.7.

Still accumulating the normal-matrix sums for the speed and direction terms...

Still accumulating the normal-matrix sums for the direction and offset terms...

Now I'm writing out the updated matrix rows, filling in the cross terms for the wind and direction sums.

Now I'm carrying the matrix elimination forward, with the u-row changes unchanged so the reduced entries just pick up the new additions.

Now I'm eliminating the u-variable from the system, updating the remaining five rows and folding in the wind measurement contributions to the sums.

Now I'm eliminating the g-variable from the system, which shifts the remaining rows as the same factors did before.

Now I'm eliminating the w-variable from the reduced system, starting with the a-row and its factor against the pivot.

Now I'm eliminating the a-variable against the pivot, then working through the s-row factor.

Still eliminating the a-variable and working through the remaining s and v rows.

Now I'm reducing the two-variable system for the remaining unknowns, finding the second variable to be about -0.65 and the first to come out near zero.

Now I'm back-substituting through the reduced system to recover the remaining unknowns, getting the shear-related value and the speed term, and then solving for the first coefficient from the updated equation.

Now I'm back-substituting the solved values into the updraft, drag, wind speed, direction, shear and veer parameters to get the updated estimates.

I'm checking the shear-adjusted speed at 150 m, which comes to about 6.34 against a measured average of 6.83. The drop measurements are pulling the wind speed down noticeably, but I'll trust the combined fit, keeping in mind that the linearization point is far from the solution, so I want to verify it against the comparison afterward.

I'm working through the SSE position values one by one, adding the two components at each spot. The totals come to 38.5, and the dt value is 1.44.

The drop totals add up to 31.05 for the time component, bringing the overall total to 69.5, which is comparable to the earlier figures. Looking across the drops, the horizontal offsets lean negative on most of the early ones, and the vertical and timing residuals on drop 2 and drop 8 point toward needing more drag. Those signals are mixed enough to treat as noise, so I'll accept the current parameter set and keep the alternatives in mind for a later check.

I'm leaning toward a lower altitude and lower speed to reduce sensitivity to wind and drag errors, and I'm going with a mid-range heading. That gives me a first target of heading 342, altitude 107, and speed 49.

I'm now running through the remaining targets: heading 54 at 93 m, heading 260 at 123 m, heading 86 at 48 m, and heading 300 at 112 m. Lower release altitude means less time inside the updraft, so I'm favoring the lower options. My plan is to simulate each release from its target minus an estimated displacement, then correct from the impact point.

I'm estimating the first release point by guessing the along-track distance and the wind drift, then setting the release to the target minus that displacement. For target one, heading 342 puts the along-track offset near (-20, 62), and with a rough wind drift the release lands around (471, 989). Next I'm working through target two at heading 54.

Now I'm working out the release points for the remaining targets: for target 2 I'm estimating a along-track offset of about 90 m and a wind drift, giving a release near (1196, 134). For target 3 I'm estimating the offset and wind drift for heading 260 to land near (1166, -958), and for target 4 a low-altitude release near (-1874, 122).

I'm checking the last release point for target five, which I'd placed at about (-1022, 26) from the heading-300 estimate.

Now I'm working through the pixel-offset corrections for each point, comparing each target position with its measured impact to figure out the adjustments needed.

Now I'm checking the remaining corrections, point 4 at about (-6.2, -2.4) and point 5 at (-1.4, -8.7), and working out the adjusted positions for each.

I've got the residuals for all five points now. Each one is already within about 1.5 m, so I expect one more iteration to tighten things a bit further.

I'm going to check the alternative hypotheses too: the earlier drop-only fit and the wind-measurement-favored fit. Running the corrected releases under each should show how much the landing points spread.

I'm checking whether the results hold up: all five targets fall within 0.3 m, so I'll rerun them under both H1 and H2 to see how much they spread, which is informative rather than something I need to average. That means ten calculations, with H2 using the specified wind, shear, veer, drag, and update values.
The spread is about 1 to 2 meters, which is good. Our combined H sits between those, so I'll keep the H releases and go ahead and execute the drops.
